static.title: The planet and its star
static.note: One fit of a transit and thirty velocities gives the planet’s orbit and the amplitude of the star’s wobble. The planet’s mass, radius and density also need the star’s mass and radius, which are stated, not fitted. Change what is stated and see how much of each uncertainty is the star’s.

samples.label: The system
samples.value: Synthetic: a light curve of four transits and 30 velocities from two instruments, fitted together with one period and one epoch (jitter 2.3 m/s, chi-square 978 for 1026 degrees of freedom). Not a real star.

samples.label: The star (an input)
samples.value: Mass 1.10 solar masses plus or minus 5.0 percent, radius 1.15 solar radii plus or minus 3.5 percent, correlation 0.5. Source: stated for this investigation (a catalog-like entry for a synthetic star).

samples.label: Mass
samples.value: 0.684 plus or minus 0.024 Jupiter masses (217 Earth masses). The data alone give plus or minus 0.009, the star adds 0.023; the star holds 87 percent of the variance.

samples.label: Radius
samples.value: 1.325 plus or minus 0.064 Jupiter radii. The data alone give plus or minus 0.045, the star adds 0.046; the star holds 52 percent of the variance.

samples.label: Density
samples.value: 0.365 plus or minus 0.050 g/cm3, with the star’s mass and radius inside it. The data alone give plus or minus 0.037, the star adds 0.034; the star holds 46 percent of the variance.

samples.label: Does the star fit the transit?
samples.value: The transit gives the star a density of 1.12 plus or minus 0.23 g/cm3; the stated mass and radius give 1.02 plus or minus 0.09. The difference is 0.4 sigma.

samples.label: What leaving the star out costs
samples.value: On a seeded ensemble of 100 systems whose stars were drawn from their stated uncertainty, the one-sigma interval held the truth, with the star inside it and with the star taken as exact, 61 and 23 percent of the time for the mass, 78 and 63 percent for the radius and 79 and 67 percent for the density. One sigma should hold it about 68 percent of the time; the star matters most for the mass.

samples.label: What it assumes
samples.value: One planet on one orbit, circular here; the star’s mass and radius are independent inputs with the stated uncertainty and correlation; the covariance is the fit’s, linearized. The numbers are first order; a Monte Carlo agrees to a few percent.
